mcqs.question: Why does ViewModel survive a rotation while an Activity's own fields do not?
options: ViewModel automatically writes its state to disk on every change
The Android framework retains the same ViewModel instance across the configuration-change-triggered destroy/recreate cycle and hands it to the new Activity instance, rather than creating a fresh one
ViewModel fields are stored in a special memory region immune to garbage collection
ViewModel prevents the Activity from being destroyed on rotation at all
mcqs.explanation: ViewModel doesn't stop the Activity from being destroyed and recreated — it's the ViewModel instance itself that's deliberately retained across that specific recreation and reattached to the new Activity, which is why its fields survive rotation while the old Activity's own fields are gone with the destroyed instance.

mcqs.question: A ViewModel exposes a StateFlow, and a Composable collects it with plain .collectAsState() instead of a lifecycle-aware collector. What's the risk?
options: StateFlow cannot be collected from a Composable at all without special conversion
The Composable will continue collecting and processing state updates even while the screen is stopped, unlike LiveData which has lifecycle-awareness built in
The app will crash immediately on first collection
The state will never update at all
mcqs.explanation: Unlike LiveData, which automatically stops delivering updates to a stopped observer, StateFlow has no built-in lifecycle awareness — collecting it without a lifecycle-scoped collector like collectAsStateWithLifecycle risks processing updates while the screen isn't actually visible, wasting work and potentially causing subtle bugs.

mcqs.question: A team adds offline support to a screen that previously fetched data directly from a network client inside the ViewModel. What does the Repository pattern buy them here?
options: The offline/caching logic can be added entirely inside the Repository, with no change needed to the ViewModel's calling code, since the ViewModel only depends on the Repository's data-shape API, not on how the data is actually sourced
Repository automatically adds offline support with zero code changes
The ViewModel would need to be rewritten regardless of whether a Repository was used
Repositories are required by the Android framework for any network access
mcqs.explanation: Because the Repository hides the decision of where data comes from behind a stable API, adding a caching/offline strategy is a change entirely internal to the Repository — the ViewModel's calls to it don't need to change at all, which is exactly the value the pattern provides once a second data source is introduced.

mcqs.question: Why does unidirectional data flow prevent two parts of a screen from disagreeing about the current UI state?
options: It requires every composable to poll the ViewModel on a timer
It duplicates state into every composable so they all have independent copies to compare
It doesn't actually prevent this; disagreement is still possible with unidirectional flow

State only flows one direction (ViewModel down to View), and the View has no path to mutate that state directly — every change must go back up through the ViewModel as an event, so there's only ever one authoritative copy
mcqs.explanation: Because the View can only read state and dispatch events, never mutate shared state directly, there's structurally only one place (the ViewModel's StateFlow) that holds the current value — this is what eliminates the class of bug where two independently mutated copies of the same data drift out of sync.

mcqs.question: A ViewModel is given a direct reference to its hosting Activity so it can call a method on it. What's the risk after a rotation?
options: The ViewModel automatically detects the stale reference and nulls it out
Rotation has no effect on this pattern since ViewModel and Activity share the same lifecycle
The ViewModel survives the rotation but its stale Activity reference points to the now-destroyed old instance, leaking that Activity's entire object graph and risking calls into a detached View
This pattern is safe as long as the reference is stored as a WeakReference
mcqs.explanation: Because ViewModel is specifically designed to outlive the Activity across a configuration change, holding a direct reference to that Activity means the ViewModel keeps a destroyed Activity instance alive and reachable, the same leak pattern as a static Context reference — the fix is exposing observable state/events instead of the ViewModel holding a reference back to the View.

mcqs.question: A ViewModel is unit-tested by mocking the exact Retrofit service interface it calls directly, since there's no Repository layer. What's the downside compared to testing against a Repository interface?
options: Retrofit interfaces cannot be mocked at all, making this approach impossible
Mocking a network client always requires a real network connection during tests
There is no meaningful downside; both approaches produce identical test quality

The test becomes coupled to the network client's specific implementation details, making it more brittle to changes there, versus a fake Repository that just returns canned data decoupled from how it's actually fetched
mcqs.explanation: A ViewModel depending directly on a network client ties its tests to that client's exact interface and behavior, while depending on a Repository abstraction lets tests use a simple fake returning canned data, fully decoupled from whether the real implementation uses network, cache, or both.
